findings.paper_title: Budget monitoring April 2025 - December 2025
findings.headline: Investment income is carrying the council's financial position, with £2.167 million (74% of total underspend) coming from investment outperformance expected to decline as interest rates fall.
findings.detail: The council forecasts investment interest of £7.9 million against a budget of £5.2 million (excluding EZ), representing £2.167 million above budget. Treasury returns are 4.57% against a benchmark of 4.03%. However, the council's treasury advisors forecast rate cuts from the current 3.75% (December 2025) to 3.50% in spring/summer 2026 and potentially 3.25% by end of 2026/early 2027, which will reduce investment returns.
findings.matters: The council's headline underspend of £2.929 million includes £2.167 million from investment income outperformance; removing this leaves only £762,000 of service-level underspend, which is fragile. The declining rate environment will eliminate this benefit.
findings.figures: £2.167 million investment income above budget; treasury returns 4.57% vs 4.03% benchmark; forecasted rates 3.75% to 3.50% to 3.25%
findings.quote: The MUFG Corporate Markets forecast below has been revised to price in a rate cut in the spring/summer of 2026 to 3.50 per cent, and then a further possible rat cut to 3.25 per cent towards the end of the year/early 2027.

findings.paper_title: Budget monitoring April 2025 - December 2025
findings.headline: The Ocella system implementation project is overrunning, driving higher than expected agency costs in Planning.
findings.detail: Planning forecasts an overspend partly due to covering vacancies but significantly due to additional work required for the Ocella system implementation. The paper explicitly states the project is overrunning and the associated agency costs are higher than originally expected, though no separate cost figure is disclosed.
findings.matters: System implementation overruns indicate project delivery and change management risks; such risks could extend to other council services and signal capability issues.
findings.figures: Unquantified additional agency costs; exact amount embedded within Planning service overspend
findings.quote: Planning is forecasting an overspend because of agency staff to cover vacancies within the teams but also to cover the additional work due to a system implementation project (Ocella project). This project is overrunning and therefore these additional costs are higher than originally expected.

findings.paper_title: Budget monitoring April 2025 - December 2025
findings.headline: The council's 2025/26 budget assumed staff vacancies below 3% but actual vacancy levels have been lower, creating a £778,000 employee cost overspend.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget does not fully fund all staff costs but assumes a vacancy factor of less than 3%, which has not been met in year. The council attributes this to continued high staff retention. Finance department is particularly affected, with overspend due to long-term absence and increased workload; Planning is overspending on agency cover for vacancies. The council has corrected the assumption downward for 2026/27.
findings.matters: It reveals that the council's baseline budget assumptions were optimistic and unreliable for forward planning; the correction came during the financial year rather than during setting, signalling potential governance gaps in budget validation.
findings.figures: £778,000 employee cost overspend; assumed vacancy factor less than 3% not achieved
findings.quote: The 2025/26 budget does not fully fund all staff costs but assumes a vacancy factor of less than three per cent, which is not being met in year. The managed vacancy factor was reduced for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: App E Prudential Indicators - 26-27 Vale (1), 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Capital programme forecast to contract 92% by 2030/31, from £21.55m to £1.70m
findings.detail: Estimated capital expenditure falls progressively from £21.55m in 2025/26 to £14.60m in 2026/27, continuing to decline to just £1.70m in 2030/31. The document provides no explanation for this steep reduction.
findings.matters: Sharp capital contraction may signal financial constraints, inability to fund planned investment, or service delivery implications – all material to credit risk assessment
findings.quote: Estimates of capital expenditure 21.55 14.60 5.31 2.90 1.85 1.70

findings.paper_title: App E Prudential Indicators - 26-27 Vale (1), 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Capital expenditure in 2024/25 underperformed planned budget by £9.4m (34% shortfall)
findings.detail: The council budgeted £27.5m for capital expenditure in 2024/25 but spent only £18.1m. The document attributes this to 'slippage from the previous financial year', indicating project delays or over-optimistic planning.
findings.matters: Lenders need confidence in councils' ability to deliver capital spending; significant underspends raise questions about project management capability
findings.figures: £27.5m budgeted, £18.1m actual, £9.4m underspend (34%)
findings.quote: Slippage from the previous financial year led to the capital programme for 2024/25 totalling £27.5 million as at 31 March 2025 – the actual expenditure for the year totalled £18.1 million thus represented an underspend against that latest budget.

findings.paper_title: 2 Capital Strategy 2026-27 to 2035-36 Vale V2 19Jan26 (1), 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Capital Strategy states £13 million borrowing, but capital programme table shows £10.45 million total
findings.detail: Page 17 (section 11.5) states 'The council's current capital programme includes borrowing of £13 million to finance capital expenditure.' However, the detailed capital programme table (pages 4-5) totals borrowing at £10,450 thousand (£10.45 million) across 2025/26-2030/31. This £2.55 million discrepancy (19% of the stated amount) is not explained or reconciled in the document.
findings.matters: Lenders require clear, consistent disclosure of borrowing levels and debt requirements to assess the council's debt sustainability and repayment capacity. A material discrepancy of this size could indicate accounting errors, incomplete disclosure of the borrowing requirement, or confusion between different policy figures.
findings.figures: Stated: £13 million; Tabulated: £10,450 thousand (£10.45 million). Capital programme borrowing: 2025/26 £4,700k + 2026/27 £2,400k + 2027/28 £3,350k = £10,450k
findings.quote: The council's current capital programme includes borrowing of £13 million to finance capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Vale Cabinet Treasury Management mid-year report 2025-26, 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Interest rates expected to fall to 3.75% by year-end; current above-budget returns will not persist
findings.detail: The council's above-budget investment returns (4.68% achieved vs 4.10% benchmark) are supported by the current interest rate environment. Treasury advisor MUFG forecasts base rate will fall to 3.75% by the end of 2025-26, having already fallen from 4.50% in April to 4.00% by August. As existing fixed-rate deposits mature and are reinvested at lower yields, the portfolio return will compress.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to forecast a headwind into 2026-27 budgets. The council's investment income guidance for next year should assume notably lower available yields, not this year's elevated returns.
findings.figures: Base rate 4.50% (April 2025) → 4.00% (August) → 3.75% (forecast year-end); portfolio return currently 4.68%
findings.quote: This forecast shows an expectation that base rate will fall to 3.75 per cent by the end of this financial year.

findings.paper_title: Vale Cabinet Treasury Management mid-year report 2025-26, 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Investment income forecast £1.46m above budget, but £1.2m is Enterprise Zone funds transferring to the EZ at year-end
findings.detail: Vale forecasts investment income of £7.004m against a budget of £5.542m—a variance of £1.462m. However, the council explicitly states that £1.2m of forecast income 'will be allocated to the EZ at the end of the financial year'. This means the structural council-retained income variance is only ~£260k, not the full £1.46m. The variance is mainly attributable to higher than expected balances and above-budgeted interest rates on new deposits.
findings.matters: A finance director forecasting 2026-27 onwards needs to distinguish between one-off and structural revenue changes. Treating the full EZ income boost as sustainable would inflate the forward baseline.
findings.figures: £7,004,000 forecast vs £5,542,000 budget; variance £1,462,000; EZ allocation £1,200,000
findings.quote: The forecast income receivable relating to these investments is expected to be £1.2m for the full year and this will be allocated to the EZ at the end of the financial year.

findings.paper_title: CABINET Vale Council revenue budget report 2026-27, 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Usable capital receipts depleting to £0.488 million by March 2031, eliminating future self-funded capital capacity.
findings.detail: The five-year capital programme consumes £5.055 million of the council's capital receipts, leaving only £0.488 million (essentially zero) available at the end of the planning period. This eliminates the council's ability to fund capital investment from its own resources in future years and locks it into grant dependency or borrowing.
findings.matters: Depletion of capital reserves to near-zero signals the council has exhausted accumulated asset-sale proceeds and will be unable to finance capital without grants or debt, limiting flexibility to respond to urgent property or infrastructure needs.
findings.figures: Usable capital receipts by 31 March 2031: £0.488 million; total capital receipts deployed in programme 2025/26–2030/31: £5,055,000
findings.quote: Estimated balances as at 31 March 2031 – Usable capital receipts 488

findings.paper_title: CABINET Vale Council revenue budget report 2026-27, 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Capital programme requires £12.168 million of prudential borrowing over five years; council now incurring MRP on cash-funded capital.
findings.detail: The council's £47.9 million capital programme cannot be funded from grants (£14m), S106 (£8.5m), CIL (£7.4m), and other contributions (£0.8m). The shortfall of £12.2m requires prudential borrowing. Though currently deployed as internal borrowing against cash balances rather than external loans, the council must budget for Minimum Revenue Provision (£6,000) and is forgoing investment income by using cash for capital.
findings.matters: Borrowing need signals capital expenditure exceeds grant/receipt funding, reducing revenue headroom and creating future MRP pressure. Combined with reserve depletion, this compounds medium-term affordability risk.
findings.figures: Total capital programme £47,903,000; prudential borrowing required £12,168,000 (25.6% of total spend); MRP provision £6,000
findings.quote: as the council has a capital programme that cannot be fully funded from grants, external contributions and its own capital receipts, it is in a position where it has a borrowing need.

findings.paper_title: CABINET Vale Council revenue budget report 2026-27, 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Council is earmarking £3 million for Local Government Reorganisation merger costs, with merger date not yet confirmed.
findings.detail: The council expects to cease to exist from 1 April 2028 under government reorganisation proposals, but this date remains unconfirmed. It is setting aside £3 million in reserves for its share of transition costs, reducing budget flexibility and creating a two-year finite planning horizon. This money is expected from prior-year underspends.
findings.matters: Unconfirmed dissolution date and pre-committed transition costs reduce financial flexibility, create service continuity uncertainty, and limit the council's ability to respond to new pressures in years 1–2 of a five-year plan.
findings.figures: £3 million earmarked for LGR costs; expected merger 1 April 2028 (unconfirmed); funding from 2024/25 and 2025/26 underspends
findings.quote: it is recommended that £3 million be put aside in revenue reserves to fund the council's share of the costs of LGR and devolution. It is anticipated that the £3 million will come from revenue underspends in 2024/25 and 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: CABINET Vale Council revenue budget report 2026-27, 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Reserve sustainability parameter will be breached beyond 2026/27 without additional savings the council has not yet named.
findings.detail: The council set a 10% threshold for sustainable reserve use and is applying 5% in 2026/27 (within threshold). However, the MTFP shows that from 2027/28 onwards, balancing budgets from current estimates would require reserve depletion above this 10% threshold. Officers note they have 'begun to look at the council's expenditure' but no specific savings plan by year has been published.
findings.matters: Unsustainable reserve depletion forces either service reductions, income increases, or further reserve draw-downs—all indicators of structural deficit rather than one-year pressure.
findings.figures: 2026/27 uses 5% of general fund and unallocated revenue reserves (within 10% parameter); reserves transfer £1,360,829 out to balance 2026/27
findings.quote: Beyond 2026/27, the MTFP shows that – based on current estimates - the use of reserves would not be in line with the sustainability parameters.

findings.paper_title: CABINET Vale Council revenue budget report 2026-27, 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Chief Finance Officer states maintaining current budget robustness beyond 2026/27 'will be a significant challenge' due to funding pressures.
findings.detail: While declaring the 2026/27 budget 'prudent and robust', the CFO explicitly warns that 'it will be a significant challenge to maintain that position in the later years of the MTFP period based on likely pressures and expectations around future funding.' This contradicts stability for the medium term and signals known structural funding gaps without yet-identified solutions.
findings.matters: Direct CFO statement that the council cannot sustain current service levels from revenue beyond 2026/27 implies either undisclosed savings plans, service cuts, or continued reserve depletion to balance future budgets.
findings.figures: 2026/27 budget described as robust; 2027-2031 period flagged as facing significant challenge to maintain
findings.quote: However, and noting that LGR is pending, it will be a significant challenge to maintain that position in the later years of the MTFP period based on likely pressures and expectations around future funding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - MTFP - VALE Budget 2026-27 v1 (1), 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Borrowing costs (MRP) increase 130-fold from £6k to £790k, signalling capital borrowing decisions
findings.detail: Minimum Revenue Provision rises from £6,000 in 2026/27 to £790,000 from 2028/29 onwards. This is a debt repayment cost and indicates the council is taking on significant new borrowing in its capital programme, locked in for decades.
findings.matters: Capital borrowing at a time of reserve depletion and funding loss amplifies financial stress. Once locked in, MRP is mandatory; it cannot be cut if budgets tighten further.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - MTFP - VALE Budget 2026-27 v1 (1), 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: £100k–£500k annual savings targets are unidentified and growing each year
findings.detail: The MTFP includes in-year savings targets of £100k in 2026/27 rising to £500k by 2030/31. These appear as budget lines but are not matched to specific deliverable savings plans within this paper, indicating they are aspirational rather than committed.
findings.matters: Unspecified savings targets are a risk indicator. They show the council has identified a shortfall but has not yet defined how it will be met. Failure to deliver these targets will accelerate reserve depletion.

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - MTFP - VALE Budget 2026-27 v1 (1), 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Government funding falls by £1.6m (22%) over five years, creating structural gap
findings.detail: Government funding and retained business rates decline from £7.28m in 2026/27 to £5.71m in 2030/31. Core funding drops from £8.87m to £7.43m. This is a systemic loss of income that forces reliance on reserves and council tax rises.
findings.matters: A sustained loss of government funding cannot be offset by one-off savings or reserves forever. This structural decline in income requires either matched spending cuts or permanent revenue increases, neither of which the MTFP demonstrates.
findings.figures: Government funding 2026/27 £7,275,481 declining to 2030/31 £5,706,283; core funding £8,866,936 declining to £7,428,925
findings.quote: Government funding and retained business rates (7,275,481) (6,938,780) (6,567,914) (6,149,318) (5,706,283)

findings.paper_title: Appendix F - MTFP - VALE Budget 2026-27 v1 (1), 06/02/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Reserves depleted from £30m to £9m over five years, with depletion rate accelerating
findings.detail: Opening reserves of £30.066m are forecast to close at £8.792m by 2030/31. Annual use of reserves grows from £1.36m to £6.28m, with the use of reserves as a percentage of sustainable reserves rising from 5% to 42% by 2030/31. This pattern shows the council increasingly unable to balance without drawing down reserves.
findings.matters: A lender cannot extend credit to a council on this trajectory. Reserves of under £9m with 42% annual depletion rates indicate the council will become insolvent unless structural funding changes or savings are found and delivered.
findings.figures: Opening reserves £30,066k; closing reserves 2030/31 £8,792k; use of reserves 2026/27 £1,361k rising to 2030/31 £6,280k; use as percentage 5% rising to 42%
findings.quote: Closing GFB and unallocated reserves 28,705 25,083 20,445 15,072 8,792; Use of reserves as percentage 5% 13% 18% 26% 42%

findings.paper_title: 1. VALE - scrutiny outturn report 2024-25
findings.headline: External legal services overspend of £61k for planning inquiries
findings.detail: Legal and Democratic service shows £61k adverse variance mainly due to overspending on external legal services for planning inquiries. Suggests unbudgeted litigation or planning appeal costs.
findings.matters: Indicates unbudgeted legal costs from planning disputes; suggests potential for recurring governance and planning decision challenges
findings.figures: £61k overspend in Legal and Democratic
findings.quote: Legal and Democratic are showing an adverse variance of £61,000 this is mainly due to an overspend on external legal services for planning inquiries.

findings.paper_title: 1. VALE - scrutiny outturn report 2024-25
findings.headline: Overall favorable position depends entirely on £1.6m investment income beat
findings.detail: The council's overall favorable variance of £1.5m is solely attributable to treasury management investment income exceeding budget by £1.6m (actual £6.651m vs budgeted £5.005m). Underlying service expenditure overspent by £125k. Without the investment income beat, the council would report an adverse position.
findings.matters: Financial position is fragile and dependent on investment returns exceeding expectations; would deteriorate rapidly if interest rates fall or cash returns normalize, creating structural deficit
findings.figures: £1.6m favorable investment income variance masking £125k adverse service spend variance
findings.quote: The overall financial position of the Council is a favourable variance of £1.5 million, due to the increased returns on treasury management investment income, which exceeded its budget by £1.6 million.

findings.paper_title: 1. VALE - scrutiny outturn report 2024-25
findings.headline: Garden waste income down £624k following permit scheme introduction in April 2025
findings.detail: Housing and Environment service shows £624k adverse variance mainly due to garden waste income falling below budget following the introduction of a permit scheme from April 2025. Charges were pro-rated until that point. The council describes this as a timing issue specific to 2024/25, expecting correct budgeting for future years.
findings.matters: Demonstrates revenue forecasting weakness and risk of income volatility from scheme implementation; raises questions about robustness of projections when new charging schemes are introduced
findings.figures: £624k adverse variance in Housing and Environment
findings.quote: A total adverse variance of £624,000, which is in the main due to garden waste income being down against budget due to the introduction of the permit scheme from April 2025, and current year charges being pro-rated until that point.

findings.paper_title: 1. VALE - scrutiny outturn report 2024-25
findings.headline: Employee costs overspent by £479k despite managed vacancy factor
findings.detail: Employee costs exceeded budget by £479k even after the managed vacancy factor was applied at the start of the year. Finance department alone had £95k overspend due to two additional temporary staff covering sickness and vacancies. The council reports new permanent staff are now in place and budgeted for future years.
findings.matters: Suggests persistent staffing and vacancy management issues, indicating structural cost pressure that may recur if recruitment and retention remain problematic
findings.figures: £479k total employee overspend; Finance department £95k of that
findings.quote: Employee costs show an overspend for the year of £479,000, which is net of the managed vacancy factor set at the beginning of the year.
